items.text: Can an equation distilled from a sparse neural residual, trained on real cloth motion capture, beat the best hand-designed aerodynamic fix on unseen speeds?
Law from a sparse residual network can cut cloth error on fast unseen motions by at least 15% versus best hand-designed drag.
Distilled law has at least 15% lower median error than best hand-designed drag on 32 fast recordings, interval excluding zero, no worse than black-box.
Distilled law roughly equals the hand-designed baseline (rediscovering textbook drag), or black-box residual fails to beat it; more or denser data needed, not compute.

Train a sparse neural residual inside a GPU cloth simulator on real motion-capture data [zenodo], distil it to an equation with symbolic regression, and test whether it beats the best hand-designed drag term on held-out speeds, after planted-law controls.

items.text: Do small robot policies drop rare skills because of too few samples, no spare capacity, overwriting by common tasks, or narrow memorized storage?
Rare-task success of small behaviour-cloning policies improves with width beyond a task-difficulty baseline, as in the OLMo result [huang], because common-task updates interfere with rare skills.

items.text: Gap between common-task and rare-task success shrinks as width grows when tasks are unevenly sampled, beyond the uniform-sampling baseline, and matched single-task models succeed.
The width-by-frequency interaction is near zero (under 5 points per width doubling), so long-tail failure is just too few rare-task samples.

Sweep MLP and transformer-head widths on Meta-World MT50 and LIBERO-90 with power-law task frequencies, using controls for scarcity, under-training and tuned baselines, then probe curvature edits to see whether width, rebalancing or protecting rare gradients helps rare skills.
